why_how.text: Suspension and revocation are different losses, and the same fates reach out-of-state privileges.
New drivers face their own sanction ladders, junior rules for permits and probation for adults.

scenario.text: Jay, aged seventeen with a junior license, is convicted of texting while driving.

reasoning.text: Junior permits and licenses draw one hundred twenty days for texting or cell-phone use.

result.text: Jay loses his junior license for one hundred twenty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a revoked license comes back on its own once the term ends.

correction.text: Revocation cancels the license outright, so reapplication, possibly denied, starts over after the revocation term.

memory_support.text: Suspended comes back; revoked starts over.

prompt.text: A newly licensed twenty-year-old asks how long the probation period lasts. What do you tell him?

rationale.text: Licensed adults eighteen or older serve six months of probation, and certain violations add sixty days off and a fresh probation.

narration.text: This chapter is about keeping your license once you have it. It begins with two words that are often confused: suspension and revocation. They are different kinds of loss, with different ways back. Then the manual explains the special sanctions for new drivers. Junior permit and license holders face their own rules, and newly licensed adults serve a probation period. We will cover each, then compare the two ladders side by side. Knowing how these rules work helps you see what is at stake with each violation, especially in your first months as a licensed driver.

lines.text: Suspension: license away for a time.

narration.text: A suspension takes your license away for a period of time, and then it is returned, possibly after you pay a termination fee. A revocation cancels the license outright. After the revocation term, you must reapply, and the new application may be denied. The same fates apply to out-of-state driving privileges and to unlicensed permission to drive. So the difference is in how you get back on the road: after a suspension the license returns, while after a revocation you start over with a new application. Keep that difference in mind for every sanction in this chapter.

lines.text: Sixty days: one serious or two lesser violations.
Sixty-day revocation for a repeat within six months.

narration.text: Junior permits and licenses have their own sanctions. A serious violation of three points or more, or two lesser violations, brings a sixty-day suspension. If the same pattern happens again within six months after the license is restored, it brings a sixty-day revocation. Texting or using a cell phone while driving brings one hundred twenty days. And a junior permit must be held for at least six months, excluding any suspension or revocation time, before scheduling a road test. So for a junior driver, a single serious ticket or two smaller ones already costs sixty days, and texting costs twice as long.

lines.text: Six months of probation at eighteen and up.
Certain violations: sixty days off, fresh probation.
Repeat round: revocation of six months or more.

narration.text: Licensed adults aged eighteen or older serve six months of probation. During probation, DWAI, speeding, reckless driving, tailgating, speed contests, or any two violations trigger a sixty-day suspension and a fresh six-month probation. A repeat round revokes the license for at least six months, with probation after it is restored. Texting or cell-phone use costs one hundred twenty days. So the probation period is a six-month window in which certain violations bring quick consequences, and a second round brings revocation rather than another suspension.

lines.text: Both revoke only after repeated failure.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People blur the junior rules and the adult probation rules. The manual contrasts them. Junior sanctions fire per violation pattern, while adult probation watches a six-month window, and both ladders end in revocation only after repeated failure. There is a second contrast too: suspension borrows the license back after a wait, while revocation destroys it and forces reapplication, and junior violations stack sixty-day clocks whereas texting jumps straight to one hundred twenty days. So ask which driver you are, junior or adult on probation, and whether this is a first round or a repeat.

Here is a quick check: a newly licensed driver aged twenty asks how long his probation period lasts. What do you tell him? Work it out before reading on. The answer is six months. Licensed adults eighteen or older serve six months of probation. During that time, DWAI, speeding, reckless driving, tailgating, speed contests or any two violations bring sixty days off plus a fresh six-month probation, and a repeat round revokes at least six months. Texting costs one hundred twenty days. If you answered sixty days, that is the suspension a violation triggers, not the probation itself.

To close, a suspension takes the license away for a time before return, possibly with a termination fee, while a revocation cancels it so reapplication, possibly denied, starts over after the term. Junior permits and licenses draw a sixty-day suspension for a serious violation or two lesser ones, a sixty-day revocation for a repeat within six months of restoration, and one hundred twenty days for texting, and the permit is held at least six months, excluding suspension or revocation time, before scheduling a road test. Licensed adults serve six months of probation, with sixty days off for listed violations. Next we turn to tickets.

why_how.text: Every ticket must be answered, in the right court.
Out-of-state offenses affect a New York license in specific ways.

scenario.text: Sam gets a speeding ticket while visiting another state and decides to ignore it.

reasoning.text: Ignoring an out-of-state moving ticket suspends the New York license until answered and proven satisfied, except for a listed group of states.

result.text: Sam answers the ticket to keep his New York license from being suspended.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an out-of-state ticket cannot affect a New York license because the conviction will not be recorded.

correction.text: Out-of-state convictions are mostly not recorded, yet ignoring an out-of-state ticket still suspends.

memory_support.text: Answer every ticket, here or away.

prompt.text: Which out-of-state moving convictions of a non-commercial licensee go on a New York record?

answer.text: Only offenses in Ontario and Quebec.

rationale.text: Those two provinces are also the only ones that feed the violation-point record.

narration.text: This lesson is about traffic tickets and what happens to them. First, the duty to answer every ticket, and where tickets are handled, both in the city and elsewhere in the state. Then the rules for offenses outside New York: which out-of-state convictions go on your New York record, what happens if you ignore a ticket from another state, and how out-of-state alcohol, drug and fatal-driving convictions affect your New York license. Some of these rules seem to point in opposite directions, so we will compare them directly before checking your understanding at the end.

lines.text: Or indefinite suspension, possible default conviction.
City non-criminal cases: Traffic Violations Bureau.

narration.text: If you get a ticket, you must answer it promptly. If you do not, your license faces indefinite suspension, and you may be convicted by default. In the city, tickets for non-criminal moving violations go through the Traffic Violations Bureau, while criminal driving charges stay in the regular courts. Outside the city, traffic cases land in the city, county, town or village criminal and traffic court where the offense happened. And every ticketed motorist may mount a defense with a lawyer. So the first rule is never to let a ticket sit unanswered, wherever it was issued.

lines.text: Mostly not recorded for non-commercial licensees.
Only those two feed the point record.

narration.text: For drivers with non-commercial licenses, moving convictions from outside New York go unrecorded, with one exception: offenses in Ontario and Quebec. Those are the only two places whose offenses feed the New York violation-point record. So a moving conviction in most other places will not show up on your New York record or add points to it. But that is only half the story. The next slide shows that ignoring a ticket from another state is a different matter, and it can cost you your New York license even when the conviction itself would never be recorded.

lines.text: Suspends the New York license until answered.
A listed group of states is excepted.
New York summons ignored elsewhere: suspension there.

narration.text: If you ignore a moving ticket from another state, your New York license is suspended until you answer the ticket and prove it has been satisfied. The manual lists a group of states whose tickets are excepted: Alaska, California, Michigan, Montana, Oregon, Virginia and Wisconsin. It works the other way too: drivers from other states who ignore a New York summons face suspension at home. So ignoring a ticket is never safe, even when it comes from another state, and even though most out-of-state convictions will not appear on your New York record.

Here is the trap. Because most out-of-state convictions are not recorded, people conclude that out-of-state tickets do not matter. The manual calls these opposite rules. Out-of-state convictions vanish except from Ontario and Quebec, yet ignoring any out-of-state ticket still suspends. So recording and answering are separate questions. Will the conviction go on your New York record? Usually not. Must you answer the ticket? Yes, or your New York license can be suspended until you do. Keep the two questions apart, and never use the first answer to settle the second one.

lines.text: Alcohol or drug conviction elsewhere: revocation.

narration.text: Some out-of-state convictions do reach your New York license directly. An alcohol or drug driving conviction in another state or in Canada revokes a New York license for at least ninety days if you are twenty-one or older. Below that age, the revocation is at least one year or until you turn twenty-one, whichever is longer. And a conviction in any state for criminal negligence, homicide or assault arising from fatal driving revokes the license, and possibly your registrations too. So for these serious offenses, where it happened does not protect your New York license.

lines.text: Which ones go on your record?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: which out-of-state moving convictions of a non-commercial licensee go on a New York driving record? Work it out before reading on. The answer is only offenses in Ontario and Quebec, which are also the only ones that feed the violation-point record. Remember, though, that this is about recording, not answering. Ignoring a moving ticket from another state can still suspend your New York license until you answer it and prove it satisfied. And an out-of-state alcohol or drug driving conviction revokes the New York license for at least ninety days from age twenty-one up.

To wrap up, ticketed drivers must answer promptly or face indefinite suspension and possible default conviction. City non-criminal moving tickets go through the Traffic Violations Bureau, other cases go to the local court where the offense happened, and every motorist may defend with a lawyer. Out-of-state moving convictions of non-commercial licensees go unrecorded except from Ontario and Quebec. Ignoring an out-of-state moving ticket suspends the New York license until answered and satisfied, except for listed states. Out-of-state alcohol or drug convictions revoke at least ninety days from twenty-one up. Next come alcohol and drug sanctions.

why_how.text: Alcohol and drug offenses carry mandatory sanctions that rise with the level of the offense.
Refusing a chemical test and Zero Tolerance carry their own sanctions.

scenario.text: Kai, aged nineteen, is stopped and has a blood alcohol level of point-zero-four.

reasoning.text: Zero Tolerance suspends under-twenty-one licenses six months for blood alcohol from point-zero-two to point-zero-seven.

result.text: Kai's license is suspended for six months.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking refusing the test is a way to avoid a worse sanction under Zero Tolerance.

correction.text: Refusing the Zero Tolerance test costs a full year, while the violation itself costs six months.

memory_support.text: Refusal costs more than the sip.

prompt.text: Under Zero Tolerance, what blood alcohol range brings a six-month suspension for a driver under twenty-one?

rationale.text: That is a level one drink can reach, and refusing the test would cost a full year instead.

narration.text: This lesson covers the sanctions for alcohol and drug offenses. The manual sets out a ladder of mandatory sanctions for driving after drinking or using drugs, a separate set of sanctions for refusing a chemical test, extra rules for drivers under twenty-one, and the Zero Tolerance law. Many of these numbers are similar, so we will compare the refusal ladder with the violation ladder, and Zero Tolerance with refusing its test. The numbers here are minimums set by the manual, and they apply alongside the fines and assessments covered in a later lesson of this chapter.

lines.text: Aggravated DWI, point-one-eight: a year or more.
DWI, point-zero-eight: six months or more.

narration.text: The alcohol and drug violations form a ladder. Aggravated DWI, at point-one-eight blood alcohol, revokes the license for at least one year. Plain DWI, at point-zero-eight, revokes for at least six months. Alcohol-impaired driving suspends for ninety days. Drug-impaired driving revokes for at least six months. And an out-of-state DUI revokes for ninety days to six months, depending on the conviction. So the higher the blood alcohol level and the more serious the offense, the longer the minimum sanction. Notice that alcohol-impaired driving is a suspension, while the others on the list are revocations.

lines.text: Past twenty-one: at least one year.
With a recent refusal or violation: eighteen months.
Under twenty-one: one year, then longer.

narration.text: Refusing a chemical test carries its own revocation. Past age twenty-one, it is at least one year. With a refusal or an alcohol or drug violation inside five years, it is eighteen months. For a first refusal under twenty-one, it is at least one year. For a second, it is until twenty-one or one year, whichever is longer. And a Zero Tolerance refusal costs at least one year. So refusing the test is not a way out. It brings at least a year off the road in every case, and more for drivers with recent history. Every refusal on this list costs at least one year.

lines.text: Refusals scale with age and history.
Violations scale with substance and level.

narration.text: Here is the trap. With two sets of numbers, people mix up the refusal sanctions and the violation sanctions. The manual explains how each one scales. Refusals scale with age and history, from one year to eighteen months to until twenty-one. Violations scale with substance, from the ninety-day DWAI suspension up to the year-long aggravated revocation. So for a refusal, ask how old the driver is and whether there is a recent refusal or violation. For a violation, ask what the offense was and at what blood alcohol level. Each ladder answers a different question.

lines.text: Listed conviction under twenty-one: a year or more.

narration.text: Drivers under twenty-one face extra rules. An arrest ending in any listed alcohol or drug conviction revokes at least one year, and a second while still under twenty-one runs one year or until twenty-one, whichever is longer, with youthful-offender and out-of-state cases counting the same. Under Zero Tolerance, a blood alcohol level from point-zero-two to point-zero-seven suspends an under-twenty-one license for six months. The manual notes that one drink can reach that level. A second Zero Tolerance offense revokes one year or until twenty-one, whichever is longer.

lines.text: Refusing its test: a full year.

narration.text: Here is a second trap. Some young drivers think refusing the test is safer than taking it. The manual says otherwise. Zero Tolerance punishes the low band, point-zero-two to point-zero-seven, with six months off, while refusing its test costs a full year. So refusal dwarfs the underlying sip. A driver who refuses ends up with twice the time off the road that the low-level offense itself would bring. That is the point of comparing the two: under Zero Tolerance, the refusal sanction is the heavier one, a full year against six months.

Here is a quick check: under Zero Tolerance, what blood alcohol range brings a six-month suspension for a driver under twenty-one? Work it out before reading on. The answer is from point-zero-two to point-zero-seven, a level the manual says one drink can reach. A second Zero Tolerance offense revokes one year or until twenty-one, whichever is longer. And refusing the Zero Tolerance test costs at least a full year, twice the six months for the offense itself. If you answered point-zero-eight, that is the plain DWI level, which revokes for at least six months.

lines.text: Refusals scale with age and history.

narration.text: To close, aggravated DWI at point-one-eight revokes at least one year, plain DWI at point-zero-eight at least six months, alcohol-impaired driving suspends ninety days, and drug-impaired driving revokes at least six months. Refusing a chemical test revokes at least one year past twenty-one and eighteen months with a recent refusal or violation. Under twenty-one, a listed conviction revokes at least one year. Zero Tolerance suspends six months for point-zero-two to point-zero-seven, and refusing its test costs a full year. Underage drinking also reaches motorboat and snowmobile privileges. Next come other mandatory sanctions.

why_how.text: Repeated violations and certain single acts revoke the license.
Uninsured driving, unpaid obligations and driving while suspended all carry sanctions.

scenario.text: Dee has three speeding tickets with offense dates inside eighteen months.

reasoning.text: Revocation of at least six months follows three speeding or misdemeanor traffic violations within eighteen months, dated by offense.

result.text: Dee's license is revoked for at least six months.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a fatal crash cannot affect your license unless you were charged with a violation.

correction.text: A fatal crash can suspend or revoke after a hearing even with no violation charged at the scene.

memory_support.text: Three in eighteen, uninsured a year, suspended driving is a crime.

prompt.text: What is the minimum revocation for driving, lending or crashing an uninsured vehicle?

rationale.text: Uninsured driving, lending or crashing revokes at least one year, and lapsed coverage means surrendering plates.

title.text: More ways to lose a license

narration.text: This lesson covers the other mandatory sanctions in the chapter, beyond alcohol and drugs. Repeated speeding or traffic violations, school bus passings and certain single acts like leaving an injury scene or a speed contest can revoke a license. Driving uninsured revokes too. Some failures, like unpaid child support, bring a suspension with no end date until they are fixed. A fatal crash can cost the license even without a charged violation. And driving while suspended or revoked is itself a crime. We will take each in turn, then check your understanding with an insurance question.

lines.text: Three bus passings in three years.
One scene-leaving or one speed contest.

narration.text: A revocation of at least six months follows three speeding or misdemeanor traffic violations within eighteen months, dated by the offense date. It also follows three passings of a stopped school bus within three years, one leaving of an injury or fatal crash scene, or one speed contest. A second speed contest within twelve months stretches the revocation to at least one year. So some sanctions come from a pattern of repeats, while others come from a single serious act. Note that the eighteen-month count runs from the offense dates, not from the conviction dates.

lines.text: Uninsured driving or lending: a year or more.
Unpaid support or taxes: indefinite suspension.

narration.text: Driving or lending an uninsured vehicle, or crashing uninsured, revokes the license for at least one year. Lapsed coverage means surrendering the plates and registration, and even parked off-road vehicles still need their plates returned, or civil and suspension penalties follow. Separately, failing to file a crash report, pay child support, pay taxes, or satisfy a court judgment from a crash suspends the license indefinitely, until the underlying problem is fixed. So these suspensions have no set end date. They end when you take care of whatever caused them.

lines.text: A fatal crash can suspend or revoke.
After a hearing, even with no charge.

narration.text: The manual notes that the word preventable crashes has replaced accidents in its vocabulary. A fatal crash can lead to a suspension or revocation after a hearing, even if no violation was charged at the scene. So the absence of a ticket does not mean the license is safe after a crash that killed someone. The hearing can still result in losing the license. This rule sits alongside the revocation for leaving an injury or fatal crash scene from the earlier slide, which applies after a single occurrence, and both show how seriously crashes involving injury or death are treated.

lines.text: A crime: fines of two hundred to five thousand.
Worse when intoxicated or with many suspensions.

narration.text: Driving while your license is suspended or revoked is a crime. Fines run from two hundred to five thousand dollars, plus possible jail or probation and seizure of the vehicle. It is worse if you are intoxicated while on an alcohol-related suspension. It is severe past ten suspensions for ignoring tickets, and past twenty such suspensions it is criminal even if you were not driving at the time of arrest. So driving during a suspension does not just extend the problem. It turns a license sanction into a criminal case, with penalties that grow with the circumstances.

title.text: When the count is the crime

narration.text: Here is the trap. People assume the crime is only in the act of driving while suspended. The manual adds a twist. Driving suspended is criminal, with fines, jail risk and seizure, and twenty ignored-ticket suspensions make it criminal even for someone who is not driving, so the count itself becomes the crime. So a person with a long string of suspensions for ignored tickets can face a criminal charge even when stopped as a non-driver. The safest course is the rule from the tickets lesson: answer every ticket, so these suspensions never pile up in the first place.

Here is a quick check: what is the minimum revocation for driving, lending or crashing an uninsured vehicle? Work it out before reading on. The answer is at least one year. Lapsed coverage also means surrendering the plates and registration, and parked off-road vehicles still need their plates returned, or civil and suspension penalties follow. If you answered six months, that is the minimum revocation for three speeding or misdemeanor traffic violations within eighteen months, or for a single speed contest. The uninsured revocation is longer, at least a full year.

To close, revocation of at least six months follows three speeding or misdemeanor traffic violations within eighteen months dated by offense, three stopped-school-bus passings within three years, one injury or fatal scene-leaving, or one speed contest, with a second contest inside twelve months stretching to a year. Uninsured driving, lending or crashing revokes at least one year. Skipped crash reports, child support, taxes or crash judgments suspend indefinitely. A fatal crash can suspend or revoke after a hearing. Driving suspended or revoked is criminal, and past twenty ignored-ticket suspensions even a non-driver is charged.

title.text: The point system and crash course

why_how.text: The point system targets persistent violators, and points add up toward a suspension.
The crash-prevention course gives limited relief.
The point table pairs violations with point values, such as eleven for a chemical-test refusal.

scenario.text: Lou has eleven points from offenses within the last twenty-four months.

reasoning.text: Eleven or more points within twenty-four months brings a mailed suspension notice, and the only hearing argument is mistaken identity.

result.text: Lou receives a suspension notice and cannot argue hardship at the hearing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the crash-prevention course can stop a mandatory suspension.

correction.text: The course cuts up to four points and some premiums but never halts a mandatory sanction, banks no future credit, and shrinks no assessment.

memory_support.text: Eleven in twenty-four suspends; the course gives relief, not rescue.

prompt.text: How many points does a chemical-test refusal carry in the table?

rationale.text: The table pairs aggravated unlicensed operation and chemical-test refusals at eleven points.

title.text: Points and how they add up

lines.text: Values, thresholds and the crash course.

narration.text: This lesson explains the point system. The manual describes what it is for, how points are assigned through a table of violations, and how the points add up. Then it gives the threshold that brings a suspension notice and what you may argue at the hearing. Finally, it describes an approved crash-prevention course, what it can do for you, and what it cannot. The course is often misunderstood, so we will be clear about its limits. By the end you will know the main point values and the key threshold, and the difference between relief and rescue.

lines.text: Fines come on top of sanctions.

narration.text: The point system hunts persistent violators through a table of violations, and the table also governs public parking lots. A single violation on its own rarely forces action, except for alcohol, drug or aggravated unlicensed cases. And every vehicle and traffic violation adds fines on top of any license sanction. So the system is designed to catch drivers who keep breaking the rules, by adding up points over time. One ticket usually will not lead to a suspension by itself, but a pattern of tickets can, and certain serious single violations are treated differently.

The table plainly pairs certain violations with point values. Texting while driving, facilitating aggravated unlicensed operation, and leaving an injury scene each carry five points. Speeding in a construction zone carries eight. Aggravated unlicensed operation and chemical-test refusals carry eleven. A child-restraint violation carries three, and inadequate brakes on an employer's vehicle carries four. The same table also rates reckless driving, school bus passing, railroad crossings, signal and sign disobedience, passing and lane faults, property-damage leaving, and most other moving violations.

lines.text: From one-to-ten over to over forty.
Points count from the offense date.

narration.text: Speeding is not a single entry in the table. It is split into bands, from one to ten miles over the limit up through more than forty miles over. Points count from the date of the offense, not from the date you are convicted. If you collect eleven or more points within twenty-four months, a suspension notice is mailed to you. At the hearing, the only argument allowed is mistaken identity. You cannot re-argue whether you were guilty, and you cannot plead hardship. So the timing runs from the offense dates, and the threshold is eleven points in twenty-four months.

lines.text: Limits: no sanction stopped, no credit banked.

narration.text: An approved crash-prevention course can cut up to four points from your record and ten percent from your liability and collision insurance premiums. But it has firm limits. It never stops a mandatory sanction. It banks no credit for the future. And it does not trim a driver responsibility assessment. So the course is useful for lowering points and premiums, but it cannot rescue you from a sanction the rules require. If you are facing a mandatory suspension or revocation, taking the course will not change that outcome, and it will not reduce the assessment bills.

lines.text: No banked credit, no assessment cut.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think the crash-prevention course is a way out of any trouble on their record. The manual says the course erases points and premiums but never halts a mandatory sanction, banks no future credit, and shrinks no assessment, so relief and rescue differ. Relief means fewer points and lower premiums. Rescue would mean escaping a sanction, and the course does not provide that. So if a question asks whether the course can stop a required suspension, the answer is no. If it asks whether the course can cut points, the answer is yes, up to four.

Here is a quick check: how many points does a chemical-test refusal carry in the table? Work it out before reading on. The answer is eleven points, the same as aggravated unlicensed operation. Texting while driving carries five points and speeding in a construction zone carries eight. Remember too that eleven or more points within twenty-four months brings a mailed suspension notice, counted from the offense dates. So a single refusal reaches that eleven-point threshold on its own, and the crash-prevention course cannot stop a mandatory sanction once it applies.

lines.text: The course offers relief, not rescue.

narration.text: To wrap up, the point system hunts persistent violators through a violation table that also governs public parking lots, single violations rarely force action except alcohol, drug or aggravated unlicensed cases, and fines come on top of sanctions. Texting is five points, construction-zone speeding eight, aggravated unlicensed operation and refusals eleven, and speeding is split into bands. Points count from the offense date, eleven or more within twenty-four months brings a mailed suspension notice, and the hearing hears only mistaken identity. The crash course cuts up to four points and ten percent of premiums, but never stops a mandatory sanction.

why_how.text: Getting a license back can cost termination fees, reapplication fees and civil penalties.
Responsibility assessments are yearly bills on top of all other fines.

scenario.text: Max has a DWI conviction and also reached six points within eighteen months.

reasoning.text: DWI triggers two hundred fifty dollars a year for three years, and six points trigger one hundred dollars a year for three years plus twenty-five per extra point.

result.text: Max owes on both assessment tracks at once.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking six points in eighteen months brings a suspension, like eleven points in twenty-four.

correction.text: Eleven points in twenty-four months suspends by mail, while six points in eighteen months bills money instead.

memory_support.text: Two fifty for alcohol, one hundred plus per point for points.

prompt.text: A driver is convicted of DWI. Which yearly assessment will follow, and for how long?

answer.text: Two hundred fifty dollars a year for three years.

rationale.text: It comes on top of all other fines, and non-payment suspends every credential.

lines.text: Fees to end suspensions and revocations.

narration.text: This lesson covers the money side of sanctions. The manual lists fees you pay to end a suspension or to reapply after a revocation, the stop-arm camera fines for passing a stopped school bus, civil penalties due before relicensing after certain revocations, and driver responsibility assessments, which are yearly bills for certain offenses. Two of these work on separate tracks and can both apply to the same driver, and there are two point clocks with very different consequences. We will compare those carefully. All of these come on top of the fines a court imposes for the violation itself.

lines.text: Zero Tolerance: penalty plus termination fee.

narration.text: A fixed-term suspension ends only after you pay a fifty-dollar termination fee. A Zero Tolerance suspension requires a one-hundred-twenty-five-dollar civil penalty plus a one-hundred-dollar termination fee. After a revocation, you usually pay a one-hundred-dollar reapplication fee. That fee is waived for revocations due to no insurance and for conditional or restricted-use licenses. So a suspension ends with a termination fee, while a revocation usually ends with a reapplication fee. Keep the two words apart: termination goes with suspension, and reapplication goes with revocation.

lines.text: Uninsured operation or crashes: seven fifty.
Refusals: five hundred, or five fifty commercial.

narration.text: Before you can be relicensed after a revocation, certain civil penalties must be paid. Uninsured operation or crashes cost seven hundred fifty dollars. A chemical-test refusal costs five hundred dollars, or five hundred fifty in a commercial vehicle. A refusal with a repeat alcohol offense within five years costs seven hundred fifty. The manual contrasts the no-insurance case with refusals: no-insurance revocations pair a year off with a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar penalty, while refusals pair revocation with five hundred, or seven hundred fifty on a five-year repeat.

lines.text: Aggravated DWI, DWI, DWAI, or refusal.
Two hundred fifty dollars a year for three years.

narration.text: Aggravated DWI, DWI, any DWAI variant, or a chemical-test refusal each trigger a driver responsibility assessment of two hundred fifty dollars a year for three years. This assessment comes on top of all other fines, and if you do not pay it, every credential you hold is suspended. So the total cost of an alcohol offense includes the court's fine, any civil penalty before relicensing, and this yearly assessment. It applies regardless of how many points you have, which is why it is described as a separate track from the point-based assessment on the next slide.

lines.text: One hundred a year for three years.
Plus twenty-five per extra point yearly.

narration.text: Six points within eighteen months trigger a different assessment: one hundred dollars a year for three years, plus twenty-five dollars per extra point per year. The assessment sometimes reaches motorboat and snowmobile cases too. And no crash-prevention course shrinks it. So the point assessment depends on your point total, while the alcohol assessment depends on the offense. The two are separate tracks, so one driver can owe on both at the same time. A driver with a DWI and six points in eighteen months would pay both the alcohol assessment and the point assessment.

lines.text: Six in eighteen months: a bill.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two different point counts appear in this chapter, and people swap them. The manual calls them two point clocks with two different teeth. Eleven points in twenty-four months suspends by mail, with hearings limited to mistaken identity. Six points in eighteen months bills money instead. So six points does not suspend your license. It brings the yearly assessment. Eleven points brings the suspension notice. Match the number and the time window together: eleven with twenty-four months and a suspension, six with eighteen months and a bill.

Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted of DWI. What responsibility assessment follows? Work it out before reading on.
